relevance_reason: Reports a CRYGC nonsense mutation segregating with autosomal dominant congenital nuclear cataract and microcornea in a Chinese family, which directly characterizes CTRCT2.

findings.statement: Guo et al. (2012) described a 4-generation Chinese family in which 6 members had isolated bilateral autosomal dominant congenital nuclear cataracts and microcornea. The nuclear opacities involved the embryonic, fetal, and infantile nuclei, and corneal diameter was about 9 mm in all affected members. All patients had nystagmus and amblyopia, and intraocular pressure was normal. The family had no history of related systemic abnormalities. The proband was diagnosed at age 8 years, and other affected members were diagnosed between 6 months and 13 years of age.
quotes: We investigated four generations of a Chinese family six of whose members were affected by nuclear cataracts and microcornea.

The nuclear opacities were located in the embryonic, fetal, and infantile nuclei. Bilateral nuclear cataracts and microcornea with a diameter of approximately 9 mm were consistent in all of the affected individuals.
The intraocular pressure of the patients was normal. Nystagmus and amblyopia were observed in all the patients. There was no history of other related systemic abnormalities in this family.

findings.statement: In a 4-generation Chinese family with autosomal dominant congenital nuclear cataract and microcornea, Guo et al. (2012) screened 9 candidate genes and identified a heterozygous c.471G>A transition in exon 3 of the CRYGC gene. The change converts a conserved tryptophan codon to a stop codon (TGG-to-TGA; W157X). The variant segregated with the disease and was absent from unaffected family members and from 100 ethnically matched controls. Bioinformatic modeling predicted that the variant truncates 18 C-terminal residues and partially removes the fourth Greek key motif. The authors noted that the same W157X protein change had been reported in another Chinese family with nuclear cataract and microcornea, where it arose from a different nucleotide change, c.470G>A (TGG-to-TAG).
quotes: Direct sequencing of the candidate gene cluster showed a c.471G>A transition in exon 3 of CRYGC, which co-segregated according to family members with cataracts, and was not observed in 100 normal controls.
The transition c.471G>A was not found in any of the unaffected family members or in the 100 controls.
The site of G>A transition in the previous W157X report was c.470G>A (TGG→TAG) in CRYGC. However, in our paper, the site of G>A transition was c.471G>A (TGG→TGA) in CRYGC (Table 2).

findings.statement: Guo et al. (2012) noted that 2 families carrying the CRYGC W157X change, one caused by c.471G>A and the other by c.470G>A, both had nuclear cataract with microcornea. Other CRYGC mutations had been associated with Coppock-like, zonular pulverulent, lamellar, and nuclear cataracts. The authors concluded that W157X is disease-causing and should no longer be considered a polymorphism.
quotes: The W157X mutation was not only observed in our family but also in another previously described family with nuclear cataracts and microcornea, indicating that W157X is the actual disease-causing mutation and should no longer be considered a single nucleotide polymorphism.
The previous W157X report was a c.470G>A transition and the clinical phenotype also was nuclear cataracts and microcornea. The phenotypes of these two mutations were similar.

findings.statement: Guo et al. (2012) suggested that mutant CRYGC W157X transcripts may escape nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and be translated into a truncated protein that could have dominant-negative effects. Losing the fourth Greek key motif may disrupt the symmetric structure and folding of gamma-C-crystallin and change how it interacts with other crystallins.
quotes: The mutant transcripts of this nonsense mutation (c.471G>A, p.W157X) may escape the NMD pathway and the aberrant PTC-mRNAs are translated to abnormal proteins with potential dominant-negative effects in cells.
This alteration correspondingly affects the formation of the fourth Greek-key motif in γC-crystallin, and then disrupts the highly symmetric structure of γC-crystallin.

relevance_reason: Reports a novel CRYGC mutation causing autosomal dominant congenital nuclear cataract in a Chinese family, with functional and zebrafish studies.

findings.statement: Li et al. (2012) described a 3-generation Chinese family with autosomal dominant congenital nuclear cataract.
quotes: in a three-generation Chinese family with autosomal dominant congenital nuclear cataract by sequencing candidate genes

findings.statement: In a 3-generation Chinese family with autosomal dominant congenital nuclear cataract, Li et al. (2012) identified a heterozygous c.385G-T mutation in the CRYGC gene by candidate gene sequencing, resulting in a gly129-to-cys (G129C) substitution at a highly conserved residue. Molecular modeling and spectroscopic studies indicated that the mutation impaired the tertiary structure of the protein by modifying the H-bonding network in the C-terminal domain, and it dramatically decreased thermal stability and increased aggregation propensity under high concentration, heat, and UV irradiation stresses.
quotes: we identified a novel, heterozygous c.385G<T mutation in CRYGC that resulted in the substitution of a highly conserved glycine by cysteine at codon 129 (p.Gly129Cys)
Molecular modeling and spectroscopic studies indicated that the mutation impaired the tertiary structure of the protein by modifying the H-bonding network in the C-terminal domain.

The mutation led to a dramatic decrease in the thermal stability of γC-crystallin, and a significant increase in the propensity of aggregation when subject to storage at high concentrations, heat, and UV- irradiation stresses.

findings.statement: Li et al. (2012) showed that expression of the gamma-C-crystallin G129C mutant in zebrafish caused vacuoles and incomplete denucleation of the lens, recapitulating the human cataract phenotype.
quotes: Using zebrafish as a model, we demonstrated that γC-crystallin p.Gly129Cys mutant caused the vacuole and the incomplete denucleation of lens, recapitulating the cataract phenotype in human beings.

relevance_reason: Reports a CRYGC nonsense mutation causing autosomal dominant congenital nuclear cataract with microcornea in a Chinese family. CRYGC is the gene for CTRCT2.

findings.statement: Zhang et al. (2009) studied a 4-generation Chinese family from a relatively isolated region of northern China in which 6 members had autosomal dominant congenital nuclear cataracts and microcornea, with no other ocular or systemic abnormalities. Affected individuals had bilateral congenital nuclear cataracts, a central nuclear opacity involving the embryonic, fetal and infantile nucleus of the lens. They also had small eyeballs and corneas about 9 to 10 mm in diameter. Every affected individual had visual acuity of hand movements in front of the eye, together with nystagmus and amblyopia.
quotes: We investigated a four-generation Chinese family with six members affected with nuclear cataracts and microcornea. The family resides in a relatively isolated region of northern China.

The affected individuals presented with bilateral congenital nuclear cataracts that consisted of a central nuclear opacity affecting the embryonic, fetal, and infantile nucleus of the lens (Figure 2) and with congenital small eyeballs and corneas with a diameter of approximately 9–10 mm.
Every affected individual had the same poor visual acuity of hand movement in front of the eye, and they also had nystagmus and amblyopia.

findings.statement: Zhang et al. (2009) reported that in the Chinese family autosomal dominant inheritance was supported by affected individuals in each of 4 generations and by male-to-male transmission. Penetrance appeared to be virtually complete.
quotes: Autosomal dominant inheritance of the cataract phenotype was supported by the presence of affected individuals in each of the four generations and male-to-male transmission.
Thus, penetrance appears to be virtually complete in this family.

findings.statement: Zhang et al. (2009) carried out a genomewide linkage scan in the Chinese family. The maximum 2-point lod score was 2.29 at marker D2S325 (theta = 0.0). Haplotype analysis placed the disease locus in a 19.04-cM region at 2q32.3-q35 between D2S117 and D2S2382. This region contains the gamma-crystallin gene cluster.
quotes: The maximum two-point LOD score (Zmax) of 2.29 was obtained at marker D2S325 with recombination θ=0.00.
The results of both linkage and haplotype analyses situated the disease gene in a 19.04 cM region bounded by D2S117 and D2S2382 at 2q32.3-q35.

findings.statement: In the Chinese family with autosomal dominant congenital nuclear cataract and microcornea, Zhang et al. (2009) sequenced the candidate genes CRYGA through CRYGD. They found a heterozygous c.470G>A change in exon 3 of CRYGC, which converts the conserved tryptophan at codon 157 to a stop codon (W157X). The variant cosegregated with the disease and was absent from 100 normal controls. The authors predicted that it truncates the last 17 amino acids and disrupts the fourth Greek key motif.
quotes: Direct sequencing of the candidate CRYGA-CRYGD gene cluster revealed a c.470G>A transversion in exon 3 of CRYGC, which cosegregated with cataracts in the family and was not observed in 100 normal controls.
This single nucleotide change was predicted to introduce a translation stop codon at tryptophan 157 (W157X).
The W157X mutation results in an in-frame stop codon at nucleotide 470 that leads to the truncation of 17 amino acids from the COOH-terminus of γC-crystallin.

findings.statement: Zhang et al. (2009) proposed that CRYGC mutations which disrupt lens biochemistry early in development may cause microphakia, with microcornea arising secondarily from damage to the lens.
quotes: The association between microcornea and congenital cataracts in all affected individuals indicate that mutations disrupting lens biochemistry and physiology early in development can result in microphakia and subsequent microcornea as a secondary effect of damage to the lens.

relevance_reason: Reports a family with autosomal dominant nuclear congenital cataract segregating a CRYGC R168W mutation. It also gives evidence of phenotypic heterogeneity at the CTRCT2 locus.

findings.statement: Gonzalez-Huerta et al. (2007) described a family with autosomal dominant primary congenital cataract of the nuclear type in which several members were affected.
quotes: One family with several affected members with primary congenital cataract and 170 healthy controls were examined.
we described a family with nuclear congenital cataract that segregated the CRYGC missense mutation c.502C>T

findings.statement: In affected members of a family with autosomal dominant nuclear congenital cataract, Gonzalez-Huerta et al. (2007) sequenced the CRYGA-D gene cluster and found a heterozygous c.502C>T transition in the CRYGC gene, causing an arg168-to-trp (R168W) substitution. The mutation segregated with the disease and was not found in healthy family members or in 170 unrelated controls. Although the variant was listed as a SNP in the NCBI database, the authors concluded that R168W is the actual disease-causing mutation.
quotes: DNA sequencing analysis of the CRYGA-D gene cluster of the affected members showed the heterozygous missense mutation c.502C>T in the CRYGC gene. This transition mutation resulted in the substitution of Arg at position 168 by Trp.
Analysis of the healthy members of the family and 170 unrelated controls showed a normal sequence of the CRYGA-D gene cluster.
Our data and previous report support that R168W is the actual disease-causing mutation and should no longer be considered a SNP.

findings.statement: Gonzalez-Huerta et al. (2007) noted that the CRYGC R168W mutation had previously been associated with lamellar cataract. They concluded that their family, which had nuclear cataract, was the first case of phenotypic heterogeneity specifically associated with this mutation.
quotes: This mutation has been associated with the phenotype of lamellar cataract but is also considered a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) in the NCBI database.
This is the first case of phenotypic heterogeneity in the primary congenital cataract specifically associated with the R168W mutation in the CRYGC gene.

relevance_reason: Only the title is available. It reports new mutations in gamma-crystallin genes that cause autosomal dominant congenital cataracts, which is relevant to CTRCT2. The title does not say which genes, variants or patients are involved.

findings.statement: Santhiya et al. (2002) reported novel mutations in the gamma-crystallin genes that cause autosomal dominant congenital cataracts.
quotes: Novel mutations in the gamma-crystallin genes cause autosomal dominant congenital cataracts.

relevance_reason: Reports a 7-generation family with variable zonular pulverulent cataract that was linked to 2q33-q35, along with a CRYGC 5-bp duplication found in the affected members.

findings.statement: Ren et al. (2000) studied a previously described 7-generation family in which 30 members had highly variable autosomal dominant zonular pulverulent cataracts.
quotes: A seven-generation family with 30 members affected by highly variable autosomal dominant zonular pulverulent cataracts has been previously described.

findings.statement: Ren et al. (2000) mapped the cataracts in this 7-generation family to a 19-cM interval on chromosome 2q33-q35 that includes the gamma-crystallin gene cluster. The maximum lod scores were 4.56 (theta = 0.02) with D2S157, 3.66 (theta = 0.12) with D2S72, and 3.57 (theta = 0.052) with CRYG.
quotes: We have localized the cataracts to a 19-cM interval on chromosome 2q33-q35 including the gamma-crystallin gene cluster.
Maximum lod scores are 4.56 (theta=0.02) with D2S157, 3.66 (theta=0.12) with D2S72, and 3.57 (theta=0.052) with CRYG.

findings.statement: In the family with variable zonular pulverulent cataract, Ren et al. (2000) found a heterozygous 5-bp duplication in exon 2 of the gamma-C-crystallin gene (CRYGC). It was present in one allele of every affected family member and absent from both unaffected family members and unaffected controls. The mutation disrupts the reading frame and was predicted to produce an unstable gamma-C-crystallin made up of 38 amino acids of the first Greek key motif followed by 52 random amino acids. The CRYGD gene showed no abnormalities.
quotes: a 5-bp duplication within exon 2 of the gammaC-crystallin gene has been found in one allele of each affected family member and is absent from both unaffected family members and unaffected controls

This mutation disrupts the reading frame of the gammaC-crystallin coding sequence and is predicted to result in the synthesis of an unstable gammaC-crystallin with 38 amino acids of the first "Greek key" motif followed by 52 random amino acids.
The gammaD-crystallin gene shows no abnormalities

variants.as_reported: 5-bp duplication within exon 2 of the gammaC-crystallin gene

findings.statement: Ren et al. (2000) sequenced the pseudo-gamma-E-crystallin (CRYGEP) promoter region and used allele-specific oligonucleotide analysis in members of the pedigree. They concluded that activation of the gamma-E pseudogene was unlikely to cause the cataracts. Because base changes in the TATA box were also found in unaffected controls, these changes were excluded as a sole cause of cataract.
quotes: Sequencing and allele-specific oligonucleotide analysis of the pseudo gammaE-crystallin promoter region from individuals in the pedigree suggest that activation of the gammaE-crystallin pseudo gene is unlikely to cause the cataracts in the family.
base changes in the TATA box but not the Sp1-binding site have been found in unaffected controls and can be excluded as a sole cause of cataracts.

findings.statement: Ren et al. (2000) suggested that their finding shows mutant beta-gamma-crystallins do not need to associate appropriately into oligomers to cause cataracts.
quotes: This finding suggests that the appropriate association of mutant betagamma-crystallins into oligomers is not necessary to cause cataracts

relevance_reason: Reports CRYGD mutation in aculeiform cataract and CRYGC missense mutation in the original Coppock-like cataract family, both mapping to the CRYG cluster on 2q33-35, which is the subject of CTRCT2.

findings.statement: Héon et al. (1999) mapped aculeiform cataract to the gamma-crystallin (CRYG) locus on chromosome 2q33-q35.
quotes: We recently mapped the aculeiform cataract to the gamma-crystallin locus (CRYG) on chromosome 2q33-35

findings.statement: In a family with aculeiform cataract, Héon et al. (1999) identified a mutation in exon 2 of the CRYGD gene by mutational analysis of the CRYG gene cluster. The mutation affected a highly conserved amino acid and was suggested to be associated with impaired folding of CRYGD; it was not seen in a large control population.
quotes: mutational analysis of the CRYG-genes cluster identified the aculeiform-cataract mutation in exon 2 of gamma-crystallin D (CRYGD)
This mutation occurred in a highly conserved amino acid and could be associated with an impaired folding of CRYGD.
These mutations were not seen in a large control population.

variants.as_reported: aculeiform-cataract mutation in exon 2 of CRYGD

findings.statement: Héon et al. (1999) found that the previously reported Coppock-like cataract mutation in the pseudogene CRYGE was a polymorphism present in 23% of their control population. Further analysis of the original Coppock-like cataract family identified a missense mutation in a highly conserved segment of exon 2 of CRYGC, which was not found in a large control population; the authors considered this the first evidence of CRYGC involvement in human cataract.
quotes: we observed that the previously reported Coppock-like-cataract mutation, the first human cataract mutation, in the pseudogene CRYGE represented a polymorphism seen in 23% of our control population
Further analysis of the original Coppock-like-cataract family identified a missense mutation in a highly conserved segment of exon 2 of CRYGC.
To our knowledge, these findings are the first evidence of an involvement of CRYGC

variants.as_reported: missense mutation in exon 2 of CRYGC

relevance_reason: Describes a large family with autosomal dominant congenital pulverulent cataract showing interocular variability. The family later contributed to CTRCT2 locus studies, but this abstract reports only the clinical findings, with no mapping or variants.

findings.statement: Scott et al. (1994) described a 7-generation family in which 48 of 138 individuals were known to have autosomal dominant congenital cataracts of the pulverulent type. Of 53 family members examined, 28 had congenital cataracts: 19 were unilateral (8 right eyes and 11 left eyes) and 9 were bilateral. The clinically unaffected eye in unilateral cases showed no lens opacity on detailed slit-lamp examination. Including historical data, there were 48 affected members (28 unilateral, 17 bilateral, and 3 obligate carriers who were not examined).
quotes: The authors describe a seven-generation family with 48 of 138 individuals known to be affected with autosomal dominant congenital cataracts of the pulverulent type.
Twenty-eight of the 53 individuals examined had congenital cataracts. Of these patients, 19 eyes (8 right eyes and 11 left eyes) were unilateral and 9 were bilateral.
Incorporating the historic data on patients who were not examined, we found 48 affected members (28 unilateral, 17 bilateral, 3 obligate carriers who were not examined).

findings.statement: Scott et al. (1994) found that cataract severity varied within the family. Cases ranged from a subtle unilateral zonular cataract with 20/20 vision, to bilateral inner fetal nuclear pulverulent opacities with 20/16 vision in both eyes, to dense unilateral and bilateral nuclear cataracts that required early surgery. The authors reported that the autosomal dominant gene was expressed in an apparently random way as either unilateral or bilateral cataract. To their knowledge, this was the first such family described in the literature.
quotes: Severity of the cataracts included a subtle unilateral zonular cataract with 20/20 visual acuity, bilateral inner fetal nuclear pulverulent opacities with 20/16 visual acuity in both eyes, and dense unilateral and bilateral nuclear cataracts requiring early surgical removal.

The authors describe a large pedigree with the apparently random expression of an autosomal dominant gene as either unilateral or bilateral cataract. To their knowledge, this is the first such family described in the literature.

relevance_reason: Reports the genetic basis that the authors proposed for Coppock-like cataract at the gamma-crystallin gene cluster, which is CTRCT2.

findings.statement: Brakenhoff et al. (1994) found that the locus for hereditary Coppock-like cataract (CCL) was closely linked to a particular combination of polymorphic TaqI sites within the human gamma-crystallin gene cluster. Mapping of these sites defined a 15-kb region that includes the gamma-D and psi-gamma-E genes.
quotes: The locus for the hereditary human Coppock-like cataract (CCL) is closely linked to a particular combination of polymorphic TaqI sites within the human gamma-crystallin gene cluster.
Mapping of these sites shows that they define a 15 kb region encompassing the gamma D and psi gamma E gene.

findings.statement: Brakenhoff et al. (1994) cloned the gamma-D and psi-gamma-E genes from the Coppock-like cataract chromosome. The gamma-D gene worked the same as its allele cloned from a wild-type chromosome. The psi-gamma-E pseudogene from the CCL chromosome had a cluster of sequence changes within and around its TATA box. Together, these changes increased psi-gamma-E promoter activity tenfold, raising its expression to 30% of that of the gamma-D gene.
quotes: The gamma D gene was functionally equivalent to its allele cloned from a wild-type chromosome.
The CCL psi gamma E gene contains a cluster of sequence changes within and around its TATA box.
Together these cause a ten-fold increase in the activity of the psi gamma E promoter, raising the level of expression of this gene to 30% of that of the gamma D gene.

variants.as_reported: cluster of sequence changes within and around its TATA box

findings.statement: Brakenhoff et al. (1994) predicted that the protein encoded by the psi-gamma-E gene is a 6-kD N-terminal gamma-crystallin fragment. They suggested that reactivation of the psi-gamma-E gene, with resulting overexpression of this fragment, could cause Coppock-like cataract.
quotes: The predicted protein product of the psi gamma E gene is a 6 kD N-terminal gamma-crystallin fragment.
Reactivation of the psi gamma E gene and concomitant overexpression of the gamma-crystallin fragment could be the cause of the Coppock-like cataract.

relevance_reason: Reports linkage of a hereditary Coppock-like cataract to the gamma-crystallin gene cluster, which is the basis for CTRCT2.

findings.statement: Lubsen et al. (1987) studied a family in which a hereditary Coppock-like cataract of the embryonic lens nucleus occurred in heterozygotes, using Taq I RFLPs within the gamma-crystallin gene cluster. A haplotype (P), not seen among the haplotypes found in the Dutch and English population, was present only in family members with cataract, and all affected members carried it. This showed close linkage between the gamma-crystallin gene cluster and the cataract locus, with a maximum lod score of 7.58 at theta = 0.
quotes: A fourth haplotype (P) was detected within a family in which a hereditary Coppock-like cataract of the embryonic lens nucleus occurs in heterozygotes.
Haplotype P was found only in family members who suffered from cataract, and all family members who suffered from cataract had haplotype P.
the gamma-crystallin gene cluster and the locus for the Coppock-like cataract are closely linked [logarithm of odds (lod) score of 7.58 at its maximum at phi = 0]

phenotypes.text: Coppock-like cataract of the embryonic lens nucleus

findings.statement: Lubsen et al. (1987) concluded that the linkage of the Coppock-like cataract to the gamma-crystallin gene cluster provided genetic evidence that the primary cause of a cataract in humans could possibly be a lesion in a crystallin gene.
quotes: This linkage provides genetic evidence that the primary cause of a cataract in humans could possibly be a lesion in a crystallin gene.
